# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is a cornerstone therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death, with survival benefits established across landmark trials in patients at high risk of ventricular arrhythmia [1,2,3]. For decades, the transvenous ICD (TV-ICD) was the standard of care; however, these devices are associated with a risk of complications related to transvenous leads, such as infection, pneumothorax, and lead dysfunction [4,5]. Subcutaneous ICDs (S-ICDs) have a totally extravascular design and were developed to overcome the risk of these lead-related complications [6].

## Concept and Early Experience

The S-ICD was conceived to provide defibrillation therapy without any intravascular or intracardiac hardware. The first-in-human work by Bardy and colleagues demonstrated the feasibility of an entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter–defibrillator in a series of pilot studies, selecting an optimal lead and generator configuration [7]. The principal trade-offs were recognised early: subcutaneous ICDs require much higher defibrillation energy than transvenous ICDs, and antitachycardia pacing is not possible with the subcutaneous ICD, which provides only brief post-shock pacing [8].

Initial clinical experience reinforced both promise and caution. In the largest early multicentre cohort, the purpose of the study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator in the first 118 Dutch patients implanted with this device [9]. Adverse events were more frequent in the first 15 implantations per centre, demonstrating that the S-ICD is effective in terminating ventricular arrhythmias, although there is a considerable percentage of ICD-related adverse events which decreases as experience increases [9]. A contemporaneous report in children and adults gave cause for caution in light of the limited published data regarding clinical sensing capabilities, particularly among younger patients [10].

## Registry and Cohort Evidence

Larger registries subsequently characterised real-world performance. The EFFORTLESS registry reported worldwide experience with a totally subcutaneous implantable defibrillator as early results [11], and its midterm analysis enrolled 985 patients over a 5-year follow-up, with the primary goal of determining the safety of the S-ICD by evaluating complications and inappropriate shock rate [12]. Notably, midterm performance rates on complications, inappropriate shocks, and conversion efficacy were comparable to rates observed in transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator studies [12]. A pooled analysis of the IDE study and EFFORTLESS registry further documented two-year safety and efficacy [13], and long-term EFFORTLESS follow-up confirmed durable outcomes of first-generation systems [14].

## Randomised Trials Versus Transvenous Therapy

The pivotal randomised comparison was PRAETORIAN. A total of 849 patients (426 in the subcutaneous ICD group and 423 in the transvenous ICD group) were included in the analyses [15]. PRAETORIAN showed noninferiority of the S-ICD with regard to the composite end point of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks after 49.1 months [15]. In follow-up analyses, the incidence of inappropriate shock was numerically higher in the S-ICD group, primarily from cardiac oversensing, though not statistically significant, while lead complications were higher with TV-ICDs [16]. The PRAETORIAN-XL trial subsequently aimed to determine whether the S-ICD is superior to the TV-ICD with respect to device-related complications at 8-year follow-up [17].

The ATLAS trial enrolled younger patients and those at elevated lead-complication risk; it showed a statistically significant reduction in perioperative, lead-related complications, which occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) with an S-ICD and in 12 patients (4.8%) with TV-ICD [18]. Overall, the S-ICD reduces perioperative, lead-related complications without significantly compromising the effectiveness of ICD shocks, but with more early postoperative pain and a trend for more inappropriate shocks [18,19]. Patient-reported quality-of-life analyses from ATLAS found no substantive differences between device groups [20]. Meta-analyses pooling randomised and propensity-matched data support fewer lead-related complications with the S-ICD [21,22].

## Patient Selection, Defibrillation Testing, and Programming

Because the S-ICD lacks bradycardia, antitachycardia, and resynchronisation pacing, careful selection is essential, and patients with pacing needs are ineligible [23]. The UNTOUCHED trial was designed to evaluate inappropriate shock rates in a more typical, contemporary ICD population, since previous S-ICD studies had patients with fewer comorbidities and less left ventricular dysfunction [24]. UNTOUCHED demonstrated high efficacy and safety with contemporary S-ICD devices and programming, with an inappropriate shock rate of 3.1% at 1 year, the lowest reported for the S-ICD [24,25]. Improvements in arrhythmia discrimination and programming, including the importance of avoiding T-wave oversensing, have been central to reducing inappropriate shocks [26,27]. The PRAETORIAN score, which estimates the risk of failure of S-ICD therapy using generator and lead positioning on chest radiographs, and the PRAETORIAN-DFT trial address whether routine defibrillation testing can be safely omitted [28,29].

## The Extravascular ICD and Future Directions

A newer concept seeks to combine extravascular safety with pacing capability. The extravascular ICD has a single lead implanted substernally to enable pause-prevention pacing, antitachycardia pacing, and defibrillation energy similar to that of transvenous ICDs [30]. In its pivotal study, the extravascular ICD safely and effectively detected and terminated induced and spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias, retaining the benefit of extravascular placement while providing pacing and low-energy defibrillation [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD has matured from a novel concept into an evidence-based alternative to the TV-ICD for appropriately selected patients without pacing requirements, offering comparable arrhythmia termination with avoidance of intravascular lead complications. Ongoing long-term trials and the emergence of extravascular and pacing-capable extravascular systems are likely to refine device selection further.
